card.summary: A percentage-based strength program by Jim Wendler that cycles heavy squat, bench, deadlift and press work to build muscle and strength.
card.note: Heavy lifting; form and gradual progression are emphasised by its author.

quick.overview:
5/3/1 is a strength training template created by powerlifter and coach Jim Wendler. It builds around four main lifts (squat, bench press, deadlift, overhead press) with work sets of 5, 3 and 1 reps set from a conservative training max.

For looks, the payoff is the muscle and strength gained from steady, heavy compound lifting plus assistance work. Its author presents slow progression as a core principle.
quick.how: Wendler's beginner page describes three full-body days with the main lifts plus First Set Last volume, and assistance work in push, pull and single-leg or core categories, with conditioning on other days. Weights are based on a training max that is raised only if every rep meets form standards.
quick.risks: Risks are those of heavy barbell training, such as strain from poor form. Wendler's page advises keeping form uncompromised and going lighter when in doubt.

lead: 5/3/1 is a strength program devised by Jim Wendler, in which a lifter works from a training max and progresses through weeks of work sets in 5, 3 and 1 rep ranges. It is widely discussed on T Nation, where Wendler is a well-known contributor and where members share logs and opinions.[1][2]

A beginner version on Wendler's site describes three weekly full-body sessions: squat and bench on Monday, deadlift and press on Wednesday, bench and squat on Friday, each with 5/3/1 sets plus 5x5 at First Set Last, then 50-100 reps each of push, pull and single-leg or core assistance work.[4]
Appearance-wise, people use it to gain muscle mass and strength, which shapes the physique in shoulders, back, chest and legs.

angle.text: The program organises progressive heavy lifting and assistance work, the inputs people use to build muscle. Lifters track the cycle to keep progress steady.

infobox: Squat, bench press, deadlift, overhead press

paras: Percentages are based on a training max, and work sets build toward roughly 80-85 percent of it. The training max goes up only when every rep meets form standards.[4]
Each day adds assistance in push, pull and single-leg or core categories, and Wendler's beginner page lists conditioning on non-lifting days at moderate intensity.[4]
Wendler states that the program should be run as written, that form should never be compromised, and that strength and size depend on mastering basics.[4]
T Nation threads mention Wendler and his gym, and some members refer to his seminars.[1][2][3]
